title: Fallen London Writer Guidelines, Part III: Writing for Fallen London
read: full (via fetch summarizer, not raw bytes)
claim: Failbetter's house rules for short game text: hard word caps, show through observable action, avoid cliche and stock phrases, passive voice only when useful, Victorian flavour as seasoning, time expressed through social events not light.
example: Root descriptions 30 words max, branch 20, result 100; clichés to avoid: 'black as pitch', 'it was quiet. Too quiet.'; time as 'knockers-up waking workers, factory bells'
rule: Cap line length hard; replace summary phrases ('All across X...') with a specific person, place, action; ban a named list of stock phrases; make the character's state visible, don't name it; express time and mood through human activity; use period flavour sparingly.

title: Points of light, pools of shadow (part I)
claim: Write a few vivid specific details and leave the rest dark for the reader to fill; one image can imply a whole room; hedged attribution ('they say') leaves room.
example: 'the right kinds of detail are like focal points in a painting'; the devil's glass of cognac in firelight implies the room
rule: One vivid concrete detail per line, then stop; do not describe the surrounding; anchor scenes in place/means rather than a fixed time.

title: Narrative Snippets: Parsimony
claim: Write the lit fires and leave the paths between them dark; the player's imagination is an ally. Few reusable qualities beat many bespoke ones.
rule: Do not write connective tissue between story beats; let gaps between lines carry the inference.

title: Iceberg theory (Hemingway)
claim: Hemingway: omit what you know and the reader feels it; the omission must be knowing, not ignorance.
example: 'The dignity of movement of an ice-berg is due to only one-eighth of it being above water.' / 'You could omit anything if you knew that you omitted and the omitted part would strengthen the story'
rule: Only omit what the writer could state (keep a private canon); the line shows the tip, and a line that merely withholds with no known referent is vagueness, not implication.

title: The Great Clomping Foot: Worldbuilding and Art (on M. John Harrison)
read: full (via fetch summarizer; secondary article quoting Harrison)
claim: Harrison: worldbuilding as exhaustive survey of a place that isn't there numbs the reader; writing must triumph over worldbuilding; shifting, non-catalogable detail forces the reader to read for everything else. The article also argues worldbuilding is fine when it serves the work's aims.
example: 'the great clomping foot of nerdism'; 'the triumph of writing over worldbuilding'; 'Worldbuilding gives an unnecessary permission for acts of writing.'
rule: Each detail must do work (metaphor, tension, feeling), not display setting; do not survey the world line after line; do not make details that fit together into a neat catalogue.

title: Advanced World-Building: Jack Vance's Tales of Dying Earth
claim: Vance gives a dying world in small drips: odd named places, ordinary strange goods and unexplained references, never a lecture.
example: 'molluscs from the slime banks'; 'city of fallen pylons'; 'the Valley of Graven Tombs'; 'three spiral green glass towers'
rule: Name a thing by one concrete odd noun phrase and move on without explaining; ordinary commerce and food (what is sold, eaten, drunk) imply a world better than grand history; unexplained is fine when the detail is physically specific.

title: Thoughts on From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (quotes Le Guin pp.94-95)
read: snippet-ish: fetch covered only a short quoted excerpt
claim: Le Guin: failed fantasy shows instantly in the style: anachronistic vocabulary, wrong conversational tone, heavy ornament. Her test is the Poughkeepsie swap. Her objection is inconsistency of register, not plainness as such (the excerpt does not settle plain vs elevated).
example: 'this failure, this fakery, is visible instantly in the style'; 'a bit heavy on the ichor before dinner'; 'Elfland is not Poughkeepsie; the voice of the transistor is not heard in that land.'
rule: Pick one register and keep it; no modern idiom or abstract managerial vocabulary in a dark-world voice; the swap test: change a few nouns, and if the line reads the same in another setting it is generic.

title: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (search results summary)
claim: Le Guin praises Dunsany, Eddison, Tolkien, Vance among others; she faults fantasy that is a comfortable imitation of the ordinary world.
example: 'trailer parks with drive-in movies' (paraphrase in search summary, unverified wording)
rule: Prefer lines that could only occur in this world; a line that also works as a modern thriller line is the failure.

title: What Happened Here? Environmental Storytelling (Smith and Worch, GDC 2010)
claim: Environmental storytelling lets players infer events from props and scene composition; the player's active inference builds investment. The model is photographs moving from close detail to wide view.
example: Half-Life smiley face made of bullet holes beside a dead body, half-finished
rule: Show the aftermath of an event, not the event; give the trace (object, state, position) and let the reader infer the cause.

rule: Do not volunteer history; let the reader dig.
